In mathematics, particularly in [[computer algebra]], '''Abramov's algorithm''' computes all [[Rational function|rational]] solutions of a [[P-recursive equation|linear recurrence equation with polynomial coefficients]]. The algorithm was published by Sergei A. Abramov in 1989.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Abramov|first=Sergei A.|date=1989|title=Rational solutions of linear differential and difference equations with polynomial coefficients|journal=USSR Computational Mathematics and Mathematical Physics|volume=29|issue=6|pages=7–12|doi=10.1016/s0041-5553(89)80002-3|issn=0041-5553}}</ref><ref name="Abramov 1995">{{Cite book|last=Abramov|first=Sergei A.|chapter=Rational solutions of linear difference and ''q'' -difference equations with polynomial coefficients |title=Proceedings of the 1995 international symposium on Symbolic and algebraic computation - ISSAC '95|date=1995|chapter-url=http://dl.acm.org/citation.cfm?id=220346.220383|pages=285–289|doi=10.1145/220346.220383|isbn=978-0897916998|s2cid=15424889}}</ref>

== Universal denominator ==
The main concept in Abramov's algorithm is a universal denominator. Let <math display="inline">\mathbb{K}</math> be a [[Field (mathematics)|field]] of [[Characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] zero. The ''dispersion'' <math display="inline">\operatorname{dis} (p,q)</math> of two polynomials <math display="inline">p, q \in \mathbb{K}[n]</math> is defined as<math display="block">\operatorname{dis} (p,q) =\max \{ k \in \N \, : \, \deg (\gcd (p(n), q(n+k) )) \geq 1 \} \cup \{ -1 \},</math>where <math display="inline">\N</math> denotes the set of non-negative integers. Therefore the dispersion is the maximum <math display="inline">k \in \N</math> such that the polynomial <math display="inline">p</math> and the <math display="inline">k</math>-times shifted polynomial <math>q</math> have a common factor. It is <math display="inline">-1</math> if such a <math display="inline">k</math> does not exist. The dispersion can be computed as the largest non-negative integer root of the [[resultant]] <math display="inline">\operatorname{res}_n (p(n), q(n+k) ) \in \mathbb{K}[k]</math>.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Man|first1=Yiu-Kwong|last2=Wright|first2=Francis J.|title=Proceedings of the international symposium on Symbolic and algebraic computation - ISSAC '94 |chapter=Fast polynomial dispersion computation and its application to indefinite summation |date=1994|pages=175–180|doi=10.1145/190347.190413|isbn=978-0897916387|s2cid=2192728}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Gerhard|first=Jürgen|title=Modular Algorithms in Symbolic Summation and Symbolic Integration |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |date=2005|volume=3218|language=en-gb|doi=10.1007/b104035|issn=0302-9743|isbn=978-3-540-24061-7}}</ref> Let <math display="inline">\sum_{k=0}^r p_k(n) \, y (n+k) = f(n)</math> be a [[P-recursive equation|recurrence equation]] of order <math display="inline">r</math> with polynomial coefficients <math>p_k \in \mathbb{K} [n]</math>, polynomial right-hand side <math display="inline">f \in \mathbb{K}[n]</math> and rational sequence solution  <math display="inline">y (n) \in \mathbb{K}(n)</math>. It is possible to write <math display="inline">y (n) = p(n)/q(n)</math> for two relatively prime polynomials <math display="inline">p, q \in \mathbb{K}[n]</math>. Let <math display="inline">D=\operatorname{dis} (p_r(n-r), p_0 (n) )</math> and<math display="block">u(n) = \gcd ([p_0 (n+D)]^{\underline{D+1}}, [p_r (n-r)]^{\underline{D+1}})</math>where <math display="inline">[p(n)]^{\underline{k}}=p(n)p(n-1)\cdots p(n-k+1)</math> denotes the [[Falling and rising factorials|falling factorial]] of a function. Then <math display="inline">q(n)</math> divides <math display="inline">u(n)</math>. So the polynomial <math display="inline">u(n)</math> can be used as a denominator for all rational solutions <math display="inline">y(n)</math> and hence it is called a universal denominator.<ref>{{cite arXiv|last1=Chen|first1=William Y. C.|last2=Paule|first2=Peter|last3=Saad|first3=Husam L.|date=2007|title=Converging to Gosper's Algorithm|eprint=0711.3386|class=math.CA}}</ref>

== Algorithm ==

Let again <math display="inline">\sum_{k=0}^r p_k(n) \, y (n+k) = f(n)</math> be a [[P-recursive equation|recurrence equation with polynomial coefficients]] and <math display="inline">u(n)</math> a universal denominator. After substituting <math display="inline">y (n) = z(n)/u(n)</math> for an unknown polynomial <math display="inline">z(n) \in \mathbb{K} [n]</math> and setting <math display="inline">\ell(n) = \operatorname{lcm}(u(n), \dots, u(n+r))</math> the recurrence equation is equivalent to<math display="block">\sum_{k=0}^r p_k (n) \frac{z(n+k)}{u(n+k)} \ell(n) = f(n) \ell(n).</math>As the <math display="inline">u(n+k)</math> cancel this is a linear recurrence equation with polynomial coefficients which can be solved for an unknown polynomial solution <math display="inline">z(n)</math>. There are [[Polynomial solutions of P-recursive equations|algorithms to find polynomial solutions]]. The solutions for <math display="inline">z(n)</math> can then be used again to compute the rational solutions <math display="inline">y(n) = z(n)/u(n)</math>.<ref name="Abramov 1995" />

 '''algorithm''' rational_solutions '''is'''
     '''input:''' Linear recurrence equation <math display="inline">\sum_{k=0}^r p_k(n) \, y (n+k) = f(n), p_k, f \in \mathbb{K}[n], p_0, p_r \neq 0</math>.
     '''output:''' The general rational solution <math display="inline">y</math> if there are any solutions, otherwise false.
 
     <math display="inline">D = \operatorname{disp} (p_r(n-r), p_0 (n) )</math>
     <math display="inline">u(n) = \gcd ([p_0 (n+D)]^{\underline{D+1}}, [p_r (n-r)]^{\underline{D+1}})</math>
     <math display="inline">\ell(n) = \operatorname{lcm}(u(n), \dots, u(n+r))</math>
     Solve <math display="inline">\sum_{k=0}^r p_k (n) \frac{z(n+k)}{u(n+k)} \ell(n) = f(n) \ell(n)</math> for general polynomial solution <math display="inline">z(n)</math>
     '''if''' solution <math display="inline">z(n)</math> exists '''then'''
         '''return''' general solution <math display="inline">y (n) = z(n)/u(n)</math>
     '''else'''
         '''return''' false
     '''end if'''

== Example ==

The homogeneous recurrence equation of order <math display="inline">1</math><math display="block">(n-1) \, y(n) + (-n-1) \, y(n+1) = 0</math>over <math display="inline">\Q</math> has a rational solution. It can be computed by considering the dispersion<math display="block">D = \operatorname{dis} (p_1 (n-1), p_0 (n) ) = \operatorname{disp} (-n,n-1) = 1.</math>This yields the following universal denominator:<math display="block"> u(n) = \gcd ([p_0 (n+1)]^{\underline{2}}, [p_r (n-1)]^{\underline{2}}) = (n-1)n</math>and<math display="block"> \ell(n) = \operatorname{lcm} (u(n), u(n+1) ) = (n-1)n(n+1).</math>Multiplying the original recurrence equation with <math display="inline"> \ell(n)</math> and substituting <math display="inline"> y(n) = z(n)/u(n)</math> leads to<math display="block"> (n-1)(n+1)\, z(n) + (-n-1) (n-1) \, z(n+1) = 0.</math>This equation has the polynomial solution <math display="inline"> z(n) = c</math> for an arbitrary constant <math display="inline"> c \in \Q</math>. Using <math display="inline"> y(n) = z(n) / u(n)</math> the general rational solution is<math display="block"> y(n) = \frac{c}{(n-1)n}</math>for arbitrary <math display="inline"> c \in \Q</math>.
